For the Parah is the aspect of the concealed Torah that has no revealed reason, as mentioned above. And "Torah or" [Torah is light] — this is the aspect of the Menorah, which is the m'oray or themselves, as mentioned above. And through all of this, the m'oray aish are subdued and the holiness is drawn also to the outside.

And this is: "A man is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know the difference between 'cursed is Haman' and 'blessed is Mordechai.'" For on Purim we subdue the rosh kol chutzos, which is the aspect of Haman-Amalek, the aspect of the m'oray aish. And then, the most exalted supernal light is revealed, and all the judgments are sweetened at their source, and all the klippos [husks/shells of impurity] and all the m'oray aish are subdued at their source, until they are all transformed to good.

And then, one does not know the difference between "cursed is Haman" and "blessed is Mordechai" — for at their source, everything is one, for everything is sweetened at its source, as is known. And then, all the m'oray aish are transformed to m'oray or, and then it is possible to draw close to Hashem, blessed be He, from all the places in the world — even from the most distant places, even from the lowest depths, even from within the klippos themselves. For even there, one can find Hashem, blessed be He, for there is no despair in the world whatsoever. And all of this is through the power of the true tzadik who draws everything through the otzar matnas chinam, as mentioned above.

And through all of this, we can understand why the gift has no sustenance except when it is written within it: "k'savu'ha b'shuka va'chasamu'hu b'vara" — for the essential vitality of the gift is from the otzar matnas chinam, whose essential purpose is to draw holiness to the outside, to the marketplaces and the streets, as explained above at length.

This extraordinary halacha — the longest of the Matanah series — weaves together the laws of gift deeds with the deepest themes of Breslov thought: Purim, Amalek, the four special Torah readings, the Red Heifer, Chanukah, Shabbos, and the role of the true tzadik in every generation. The legal ruling — that a gift deed requires the clause "write it in the marketplace" — becomes the gateway to a sweeping spiritual panorama:

The Treasury of Undeserved Gifts (Otzar Matnas Chinam): Before Sinai, the world was sustained by pure chesed — a concealed Torah hidden within creation. The true tzadik accesses this treasury when he nullifies himself from Torah study, becoming a "simple man." Through this, he draws spiritual life to even the most distant souls.

Amalek's War — the battle for the distant ones: Amalek targets the weak — those expelled by the Clouds of Glory. He creates confusion (machlokes) so no one knows where truth lies. The tzadik fights this war by bringing close those whom Amalek claims as his own.

Mordechai and Esther = Rosh Bayis: Mordechai is rosh (head) — the four mochin, the Name of Hashem, m'oray or (luminaries of light). Esther is bayis (house) — the Temple, malchus (kingship), the moon. Haman is their opposite: rosh kol chutzos (head of the streets), m'oray aish (luminaries of fire).

The Four Parshiyos: Shekalim = building the Temple → strengthening rosh bayis. Zachor = erasing Amalek. Parah = the concealed Torah, purifying even from the impurity of death. HaChodesh = filling the moon, m'oray or overcoming m'oray aish.

On Purim: The greatest light is revealed. Mordechai (= v'rav chesed in gematria) emerges. Everyone can draw close — even from She'ol. "Whoever extends his hand to receive — they give him." The custom of engaging in levity reflects the concealed Torah within all things. Drinking until one cannot distinguish Haman from Mordechai reflects the root-level sweetening where all judgments become good.

The legal teaching: All of this is why "write it in the marketplace" is essential for a gift — because the spiritual root of all gift-giving is the otzar matnas chinam, whose entire purpose is to draw holiness to the outside.

Based upon the Torah that begins "And it came to pass at the end [mikaitz] — for He who has compassion on them shall lead them", etc. [Likutay Moharan II, 7; cf. Isaiah 49:10] — see there. And we have already spoken about this Torah several times.

And it is explained there that every person must leave behind his da'as [knowledge / mind / awareness] in the world through sons and disciples, engaging with them to make known to them the way of G-d — and this is the essential exchange and legacy that remains from a person after his departure from the world, etc.; see there. And it is explained there that through the illumination of sons and disciples, from there sustenance [parnasah] is drawn, etc.; see there.

And this is the aspect of yerushah [inheritance] that belongs to sons — for the essential legacy a person leaves after his death is his sons, who remain after him and fill his place. And the essence is the da'as [knowledge/awareness] — meaning that when one merits it, there remain after him sons who received from him his holy da'as. For every one of Israel has a share in the holy da'as, for the essential da'as is to know G-d, as it is written: "You have been shown to know that Hashem is G-d, etc." [Deuteronomy 4:35] And every one of Israel is a portion of G-d from above [cf. Job 31:2; Tikkunay Zohar], and his soul is rooted in this holy da'as, which is the root of all souls — for Chachmah [Wisdom] is the root of all, as it is written: "You made them all with wisdom [Chachmah]" [Psalms 104:24].

And therefore, every one of Israel — according to his attachment to the holy da'as and according to his good deeds — so is the knowledge of G-d's divinity, blessed be He, revealed through him. And this is the essential legacy after his death — namely, what he made known to his sons and commanded them, that they keep the way of G-d. And this da'as is the essential legacy, as is explained in the aforementioned Torah.

And since all sustenance and wealth is drawn from this da'as — which is the aspect encompassing [both] son and disciple, as is explained there in the aforementioned Torah; see there — therefore, when a person passes away, the inheritance reaches his sons, for the root of wealth derives from the aspect of sons — meaning from the da'as he left in the world through his sons, from which all wealth and sustenance is drawn, as stated above. And therefore the inheritance reaches them, for from there the wealth is drawn, as stated above.

And this is [the nature of] a matnas shchiv mera [a deathbed-bequest gift] which is also like an inheritance. For the da'as that one must leave behind is comprised of two aspects — [that of] son and [that of] disciple — for one must leave behind sons and disciples, as is explained there in the aforementioned Torah. For just as one must teach one's own sons — to illuminate within them the holy da'as — so too must one teach another's son and establish many disciples, to illuminate within them the holy da'as to know G-d. And as is explained there in the aforementioned Torah, every person can fulfill this — to establish disciples — by speaking with his fellow about fear of Heaven, and one arousing the other to fear G-d, to turn from evil and do good, so that through this each one becomes in the aspect of a disciple to the other; see there.

And from the aspect of the da'as that one illuminates within disciples — each person according to his aspect — from there is drawn the aspect of matnas shchiv mera that is like an inheritance. For a person has the power to bequeath his wealth to another through a matnas shchiv mera, since wealth is drawn also from the da'as that one illuminates within others who are not his sons — who are the disciples. And therefore he can bequeath his wealth to others through a matnas shchiv mera, just as he must illuminate his da'as to others who are the disciples. For just as the inheritance belongs to the sons — because wealth is drawn from the da'as he left through his sons — so too can he bequeath his wealth to others, for wealth is drawn also from the da'as that one illuminates within others, who are the disciples, as stated above. For wealth is drawn from both aspects — from son and from disciple — as is explained in the aforementioned Torah.

And therefore, specifically when he is a shchiv mera [one who is deathly ill / bedridden], his gift is like an inheritance. For the tzadik, and likewise every upright person, illuminates the da'as within sons and disciples all the days of his life — for it is only for this that a person comes into the world. And the essential [goal] is to draw such a da'as into sons and disciples that it will endure forever, even after his passing — for this is the essential legacy, as stated above, and as is explained clearly in the aforementioned Torah.

And therefore, the true tzadikim, at the time of their illness, illuminate the da'as even more intensely within sons and disciples — as we find with several tzadikim who revealed a very great and holy da'as at the time of their illness, near their death — such as Rabbi Eliezer the Great, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and Rabbenu HaKadosh [our Holy Teacher, Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi], etc. [cf. Sanhedrin 68a; Shabbos 33b; Kesubos 103a]

For the essential illness that is drawn into the world — that a person is ill before his death — is only for this reason: so that he may set his household in order, "so that he may command his sons and his disciples after him" [cf. Genesis 18:19] that they know G-d and keep His ways. And therefore, until Yaakov there was no weakness [before death], as our Sages, of blessed memory, stated [Bava Metzia 87a] — for Yaakov was the first to illuminate so intensely within sons and disciples. For the beginning of the revelation of the holy da'as — to know G-d — began with our father Avraham, for he revealed G-d's divinity in the world, as our Sages, of blessed memory, stated. But Avraham and Yitzchak still did not have their bed [lineage] complete — only Yaakov's bed was complete, and he left behind twelve tribes, all of them tzadikim, all of whom received his holy da'as, and through them the holy da'as was sustained in the world.

And therefore it began with Yaakov that a person should be ill before his death — for it is a great good, so that he may set his household in order and command his sons, as our Sages, of blessed memory, stated. And the essential commandment is that one must command them to keep the way of G-d, so that his da'as will remain even after his passing, forever. And therefore this began with Yaakov, for he was the first to leave behind sons who were all tzadikim, through whom his da'as remained in the world forever.

And therefore, at the time when Yaakov was ill and commanded his sons near his death, they all cried out: "Hear O Israel [Shema Yisrael], Hashem is our G-d, Hashem is One", etc., as our Sages, of blessed memory, stated [Pesachim 56a] — for at that time, when the tzadik is ill near his death, that is the essential illumination of the da'as that he leaves behind after him, as stated above. And likewise for every person, according to his own aspect — for every person can fulfill this. And every person must illuminate some aspect of holy da'as within sons and disciples, so that it endures forever, as stated above.

And therefore, the essential gift that is like an inheritance is specifically the matnas shchiv mera — for it is then that the essential leaving-behind of the da'as occurs, from which wealth is drawn. And because of this the inheritance reaches his sons, and likewise he has the power to give to others through a matnas shchiv mera which is also like an inheritance, as stated above.

And this is [what is meant by]: "the words of a shchiv mera are as [if they were already] written and delivered" [Bava Basra 135b; Gittin 13a] — for the validity of the matnas shchiv mera is drawn from the aspect of the da'as that one must illuminate with even greater intensity near one's death, when one is a shchiv mera, as stated above. And the da'as is the Torah, which is the essential da'as through which one knows G-d, blessed be He.

And this is: "the words of a shchiv mera are as written and delivered" — "written and delivered" is the aspect of the holy Torah, which is written [kesuvah] and delivered [mesurah] in our hands. And every person, according to his portion in the Torah, so must he leave behind his portion of da'as and Torah to sons and disciples so that it endures forever. And from there is drawn the matnas shchiv mera that has validity like an inheritance, as stated above. And therefore "the words of a shchiv mera are as written and delivered," as stated above.
